evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

spec.title: Lyme Disease Diagnosis-Count Gap Simulator (CDC Claims-Based Estimate vs. Surveillance)
spec.boundary: This simulation reconstructs the case-count correction steps in a CDC dispatch (Kugeler et al., 2021) that estimates how many people are clinically diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease each year using commercial insurance claims (IBM MarketScan, 2010-2018), and compares that corrected estimate to the officially surveilled case count for the same period. It represents only the frequency/case-count burden; it contains no dollar costs, no productivity-loss data, and no demographic (sex, age, race) breakdown of the final estimate - the document itself defers that breakdown to a companion paper. The document explicitly states the gap between its claims-based estimate and the surveillance count reflects a combination of surveillance underreporting and clinical overdiagnosis/overtreatment that it cannot separate; this simulator preserves that ambiguity and does not resolve it. Federal Lyme surveillance line-list data (2008-2021, a separate passive-surveillance data source) show more reported cases among males than females over that period, but this document's own claims-based estimate carries no sex breakdown.

takeaway.patient: This CDC analysis found that roughly 476,000 people a year were estimated to be clinically diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease (2010-2018), far more than the roughly 35,000 a year counted through official public-health surveillance. That does not mean the official count is simply wrong or that the larger number is the 'real' one - the authors say the gap reflects a mix of cases that surveillance misses and some degree of doctors treating presumptively (overdiagnosis), and they say they cannot tell how much of the gap comes from each cause. If you were diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease, you are part of a group much larger than official statistics suggest, but this study cannot tell you whether your own case would have met the formal surveillance case definition.
takeaway.care: Using the document's own correction steps, an age/state-standardized claims count of about 205,000 patients/year is divided by a 43% ICD-coding-completeness factor (based on 672 chart-reviewed records from three states) to reach the ~476,000/year national estimate - compared against ~35,000/year captured by passive surveillance for the same period. The gap reflects both surveillance underreporting and clinical overdiagnosis/overtreatment, which the document explicitly cannot disentangle. A secondary finding - diagnoses skewed toward low-incidence states (19% vs. a typical ~5% in surveillance) - is noted by the authors as a possible (not confirmed) partial signal of overdiagnosis.
takeaway.policy: The document's corrected estimate is ~476,000 diagnosed-and-treated Lyme patients/year (95% credible interval 405,000-547,000) for 2010-2018, versus ~35,000/year captured by passive national surveillance - a more than tenfold difference. The authors attribute this combined gap to underreporting and overdiagnosis without being able to apportion it, and note the correction relies on a small 3-state, 672-record chart-review sample for the undercoding factor. This has implications for surveillance investment and for interpreting claims-based disease-burden estimates generally, but should not be read as resolving 'true' Lyme incidence.

patient: If you were diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease, understand that official surveillance statistics likely undercount people like you - don't assume your case is unusual just because it isn't reflected in public case counts.
If your treatment started without a lab-confirmed result, consider asking your clinician what led to that decision, since this study notes doctors sometimes treat presumptively for Lyme disease.

If you want to understand how your diagnosis was counted (or not) in official statistics, ask your clinician what the difference is between a clinical diagnosis and a case meeting the formal surveillance definition - these measure different things, and neither is automatically the 'right' one for your personal care decisions.
care: Consider auditing your own coding practices against this study's finding that only 43% of medical records meeting Lyme case criteria contained the specific ICD-9/10 code, since similar undercoding could distort internal registries or quality metrics.

The finding that 19% of claims-identified diagnoses occurred in low-incidence states (vs. a typical ~5% in surveillance) may be worth checking against your own patient population to see whether presumptive-treatment patterns vary by region - this is an observation to investigate, not a confirmed overdiagnosis rate.

When communicating diagnostic uncertainty to teams or patients, keep the two contributing causes (surveillance underreporting vs. clinical overdiagnosis) explicitly separate, since the source data cannot attribute the gap to either one specifically.
policy: Use the ~476,000/year corrected estimate (95% CrI 405,000-547,000) alongside the ~35,000/year surveillance count to scope surveillance-system investment needs, while treating the gap as an unresolved mix of underreporting and overdiagnosis rather than a single true-incidence figure.

Consider supporting the electronic medical/laboratory data system improvements the document's own conclusions call for, to address the demonstrated gap in ICD-code completeness for Lyme disease records.

## Source and scope
This simulator reconstructs the case-count correction steps from a CDC dispatch (Kugeler et al., *Emerging Infectious Diseases*, Feb 2021) estimating how many people are clinically diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease annually in the US (2010-2018), using IBM MarketScan commercial insurance claims. It also reproduces the document's own comparison against the ~35,000/year count captured through passive national surveillance for the same period (p.618). The document contains no dollar cost figures; this simulator addresses case-count/frequency burden only.

## Correction chain
The ~205,000/year standardized claims count (p.617) is divided by a 43.0% ICD-9/10 undercoding correction factor - the share of 672 chart-reviewed records (from NY, MD, MN) meeting Lyme case criteria that actually contained the specific diagnosis code (p.617) - to reach the document's ~476,000/year estimate (95% CrI 405,000-547,000). Recomputing with the document's own rounded 43% factor yields a value close to but not an exact match to the stated 476,000, likely reflecting unrounded internal arithmetic the document does not fully disclose.

## Limitations
**Claims/coding basis**: The central estimate derives entirely from ICD-9/10 claims coding combined with antibiotic-duration criteria; because the document itself finds only 43% of qualifying records carry the specific code, any claims-based count - including this one - likely undercounts true clinically-relevant Lyme activity before correction, and the correction itself rests on a small 3-state, 672-record sample.

**No subgroup breakdown**: The final ~476,000/year figure is a single pooled national estimate; the document does not disaggregate it by sex, age, or race/ethnicity in its own text (it references a companion paper, Schwartz et al. 2021, for that). Federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally support disaggregated analysis even where this document did not perform one. Separately, federal Lyme surveillance line-list data (2008-2021) show more reported cases among males (259,078) than females (194,731), but this is a distinct, passive-surveillance data source, not a breakdown of this document's own claims-based estimate.

**Systemic gap**: The document frames the undercoding finding as a data-infrastructure limitation and calls for improved electronic medical/laboratory systems and greater clinician/public awareness to support accurate diagnosis and surveillance (p.617-618).

The ~476,000 vs. ~35,000 gap reflects an unseparated mix of surveillance underreporting and clinical overdiagnosis/overtreatment; the document explicitly states it cannot discern each cause's relative contribution, and neither figure should be read as the 'true' incidence of Lyme disease.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Estimated annual number of persons diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease in the US (claims-based, corrected for age extrapolation and ICD undercoding) (2010-2018 average, the United States): the document's estimate of 476,000 is 13.6 times the 34,973 cases CDC received as reported (yearly totals ranged 30,158 to 42,743). Reported cases are a passive-surveillance subset, so estimates from claims or models are usually higher; this shows the size of the gap, not which figure is right. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- National Lyme disease cases reported annually through passive public health surveillance, as cited by the document in its own comparison (2010-2018 average, the United States): the document reports 35,000; CDC's reported cases averaged 34,973 (confirmed and probable together) (yearly totals ranged 30,158 to 42,743), so the document's figure is within 10% of the CDC confirmed-plus-probable total (+0.1% versus the total). Definitions may differ between the document and CDC surveillance, so a gap is a prompt to check, not an error. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.

spec.title: Lyme Disease Diagnosis-Count Gap Simulator (CDC Claims-Based Estimate vs. Surveillance)
spec.boundary: This simulation reconstructs the case-count correction steps in a CDC dispatch (Kugeler et al., 2021) that estimates how many people are clinically diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease each year using commercial insurance claims (IBM MarketScan, 2010-2018), and compares that corrected estimate to the officially surveilled case count for the same period. It represents only the frequency/case-count burden; it contains no dollar costs, no productivity-loss data, and no demographic (sex, age, race) breakdown of the final estimate - the document itself defers that breakdown to a companion paper. The document explicitly states the gap between its claims-based estimate and the surveillance count reflects a combination of surveillance underreporting and clinical overdiagnosis/overtreatment that it cannot separate; this simulator preserves that ambiguity and does not resolve it. Federal Lyme surveillance line-list data (2008-2021, a separate passive-surveillance data source) show more reported cases among males than females over that period, but this document's own claims-based estimate carries no sex breakdown.

takeaway.patient: This CDC analysis found that roughly 476,000 people a year were estimated to be clinically diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease (2010-2018), far more than the roughly 35,000 a year counted through official public-health surveillance. That does not mean the official count is simply wrong or that the larger number is the 'real' one - the authors say the gap reflects a mix of cases that surveillance misses and some degree of doctors treating presumptively (overdiagnosis), and they say they cannot tell how much of the gap comes from each cause. If you were diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease, you are part of a group much larger than official statistics suggest, but this study cannot tell you whether your own case would have met the formal surveillance case definition.
takeaway.care: Using the document's own correction steps, an age/state-standardized claims count of about 205,000 patients/year is divided by a 43% ICD-coding-completeness factor (based on 672 chart-reviewed records from three states) to reach the ~476,000/year national estimate - compared against ~35,000/year captured by passive surveillance for the same period. The gap reflects both surveillance underreporting and clinical overdiagnosis/overtreatment, which the document explicitly cannot disentangle. A secondary finding - diagnoses skewed toward low-incidence states (19% vs. a typical ~5% in surveillance) - is noted by the authors as a possible (not confirmed) partial signal of overdiagnosis.
takeaway.policy: The document's corrected estimate is ~476,000 diagnosed-and-treated Lyme patients/year (95% credible interval 405,000-547,000) for 2010-2018, versus ~35,000/year captured by passive national surveillance - a more than tenfold difference. The authors attribute this combined gap to underreporting and overdiagnosis without being able to apportion it, and note the correction relies on a small 3-state, 672-record chart-review sample for the undercoding factor. This has implications for surveillance investment and for interpreting claims-based disease-burden estimates generally, but should not be read as resolving 'true' Lyme incidence.

patient: If you were diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease, understand that official surveillance statistics likely undercount people like you - don't assume your case is unusual just because it isn't reflected in public case counts.

If you want to understand how your diagnosis was counted (or not) in official statistics, ask your clinician what the difference is between a clinical diagnosis and a case meeting the formal surveillance definition - these measure different things, and neither is automatically the 'right' one for your personal care decisions.
care: Consider auditing your own coding practices against this study's finding that only 43% of medical records meeting Lyme case criteria contained the specific ICD-9/10 code, since similar undercoding could distort internal registries or quality metrics.

Consider supporting the electronic medical/laboratory data system improvements the document's own conclusions call for, to address the demonstrated gap in ICD-code completeness for Lyme disease records.

Treat the low-incidence-state diagnosis concentration (19% vs. ~5%) as a signal worth further investigation into regional diagnostic practice variation, not as a quantified overdiagnosis rate, before using it in policy justification.
